title: Antibiotic Targets, Synergy Testing and the Septic-Shock Clock
summary: Learn which cellular target each major antibiotic class hits, how a checkerboard FIC index and a time-kill assay define synergy, how tolerance is expressed as an MBC/MIC ratio, and what the Kumar 2006 septic-shock timing data do and do not show.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 58 Hits 13 (Kumar 2006 septic-shock timing), 14 (checkerboard FIC, time-kill synergy, tolerance) and 21 (antibiotic targets by class). Checked against Kapoor 2017, Gajdács 2017, Stein 2015, Cázares-Domínguez 2015, Kumar 2014 and Evans 2021 (open full text), and Kohanski 2010 and Doern 2014 (each read via a page-fetch tool). The Kumar 2006 paper itself was not read (not open access); its figures are taught from its first author’s 2014 review, and the SSC 2021 guideline gives the context that the evidence is observational and weaker without shock (register flag rv-ch58-kumar-context). Doern 2014 defines time-kill synergy as a >2 log10 (not ≥2) greater kill, synergy cutoffs vary between studies, and synergy testing is not endorsed for routine use (rv-ch58-synergy-method). Tolerance as MBC/MIC ≥32 is confirmed only as a common definition in one primary study. Not taught: the Number Vault note that tolerance means bacteriologic failure despite susceptibility; the “rapid AST and stewardship” rationale; bacteriostatic labels for clindamycin and linezolid.

objectives: Match β-lactams, vancomycin, aminoglycosides, macrolides, clindamycin, linezolid, fluoroquinolones, rifampin, TMP-SMX and metronidazole to their targets.
Calculate an FIC index from checkerboard MICs and classify the interaction; state the time-kill synergy definition and the limits of synergy testing.
Define tolerance by the MBC/MIC ratio.
State what the Kumar 2006 septic-shock timing data showed and how the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline frames antibiotic timing.

scenes.title: Two drugs, one plate, one clock
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three cards on a microbiology bench. (1) A clinician asks whether ampicillin and gentamicin hit the same bacterial target. (2) A checkerboard plate for drug A plus drug B: drug A MIC 8 µg/mL alone and 2 µg/mL in combination; drug B MIC 4 µg/mL alone and 1 µg/mL in combination. (3) A patient in septic shock: hypotension began at 06:00, the first effective antibiotic was given at 10:00. Question token: “Which target, is it synergy, and does the clock matter?”

cues.text: Three questions reach the bench. A clinician asks whether ampicillin and gentamicin hit the same target in the bacterium.
A checkerboard plate shows drug A falling from an MIC of eight to two in combination, and drug B from four to one.
And a patient in septic shock became hypotensive at six, but got an effective antibiotic only at ten. Which target, is it synergy, and does the clock matter?

props.label: Which target, synergy, and does the clock matter?

scenes.title: Where each class hits
scenes.altText: Schematic: four target cards around a bacterial cell. Cell wall: β-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins and block peptidoglycan cross-linking; glycopeptides (vancomycin) bind the D-alanyl-D-alanine end of cell-wall precursors. 30S ribosome: aminoglycosides bind 16S rRNA, cause misreading and are the broadly bactericidal ribosome inhibitors; tetracyclines also act on 30S. 50S ribosome: macrolides, lincosamides (clindamycin) and oxazolidinones (linezolid); macrolides are typically bacteriostatic. Nucleic acid and folate: fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; rifamycins bind RNA polymerase and block transcription; sulfamethoxazole blocks dihydropteroate synthase and trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase, two steps of one pathway; metronidazole is a prodrug that must be reduced, releasing reactive products that damage DNA, and is a key anaerobe drug.

cues.text: Start at the wall. Beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins and stop peptidoglycan cross-linking. Vancomycin binds the D-alanyl-D-alanine end of the wall precursors.

Aminoglycosides bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and cause misreading; among ribosome inhibitors they are the broadly bactericidal ones. Cell-wall drugs help them get into the cell, which is one basis for combining them.
Macrolides, clindamycin and linezolid act on the 50S subunit. Macrolides are typically bacteriostatic.

Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase four. Rifampin binds RNA polymerase. Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim block two steps of the folate pathway. Metronidazole must be reduced inside the cell, and its products damage DNA, which makes it a key anaerobe drug.

scenes.title: Measuring synergy
scenes.altText: Checkerboard schematic: drug A in twofold dilutions across the plate, drug B in twofold dilutions down, so every well holds a different pair. For each drug, FIC = MIC in combination ÷ MIC alone; the FIC index (FICI) = FIC of A + FIC of B. Interpretation card (Doern 2014): FICI ≤ 0.5 = synergy (a fourfold MIC reduction); 0.5–1 = additive or non-synergistic; 1–4 = indifferent; > 4 = antagonism. Time-kill card: colony counts over time; synergy = more than a 2 log10 greater kill by the combination than by its most active single agent, best judged within the first 12 h. Caveat token: no gold standard; methods often disagree; not endorsed for routine clinical use.

cues.text: Synergy can be measured. In a checkerboard, drug A runs in twofold dilutions across the plate and drug B down it, so every well holds a different pair.
For each drug, the fractional inhibitory concentration, or FIC, is its MIC in combination divided by its MIC alone. Add the two FICs to get the FIC index.
In a widely cited review, an index of one half or less is synergy, a fourfold drop in MIC. Up to one is additive, one to four is indifferent, and above four is antagonism.

A time-kill assay counts survivors over time. Synergy is more than a two-log greater kill than the best single drug, best judged in the first twelve hours. There is no gold standard, methods often disagree, and routine synergy testing is not endorsed.

props.title: Time-kill
lines: > 2 log10 more kill than best drug

scenes.title: Working the numbers
scenes.altText: Worked example card: drug A 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25; drug B 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25; FICI = 0.5 → synergy. Tolerance card: an isolate inhibited at a low concentration but killed only at a much higher one; in a study of vancomycin-tolerant MRSA, vancomycin tolerance is described as commonly defined as an MBC/MIC ratio ≥ 32 (example: MIC 1, MBC 32 µg/mL → ratio 32). Clock card (Kumar 2006, as summarised by its first author in 2014): retrospective septic-shock cohort; effective antimicrobial within the first hour after onset of hypotension → 79.9% survival to discharge; each additional hour of delay over the first 6 h → survival fell by an average of 7.6%. Context card (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021): give antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 h of recognition, in possible septic shock or a high likelihood of sepsis; in possible sepsis without shock, rapid investigation and antimicrobials within 3 h if concern for infection persists; the time association is weaker without shock and the evidence is observational. Hook answers: (1) different targets, cell wall and 30S; (2) FICI 0.5 = synergy; (3) a 4-hour delay matters.

cues.text: Back to the plate. Drug A: two divided by eight is a quarter. Drug B: one divided by four is a quarter. The index is one half, so the pair is synergistic.

Tolerance is a different problem: the isolate is inhibited at a low concentration but killed only at a much higher one. For vancomycin and MRSA it is commonly defined as an MBC to MIC ratio of thirty-two or more, for example an MIC of one with an MBC of thirty-two.

Now the clock. In Kumar’s 2006 retrospective study of septic shock, effective antibiotics in the first hour after hypotension began meant about eighty percent survival. Each further hour of delay, across the first six hours, cut survival by an average of seven point six percent.

The 2021 Surviving Sepsis guideline gives antimicrobials immediately, ideally within an hour, in possible septic shock or likely sepsis, and within three hours in possible sepsis without shock if concern persists. So: different targets, synergy, and yes, the four-hour delay matters.

props.title: SSC 2021
lines: Sepsis, no shock: ≤ 3 h if concern

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Aminoglycosides and macrolides both act on the 50S subunit” (✓ aminoglycosides bind 30S; macrolides bind 50S); “An FIC index of 2 means synergy” (✓ synergy is ≤ 0.5; 1–4 is indifferent); “Survival falls 7.6% per hour in every septic patient, at every hour” (✓ one retrospective septic-shock study, first 6 h after hypotension; weaker association without shock).

cues.text: Trap one: aminoglycosides and macrolides both act on the 50S subunit. No: aminoglycosides bind 30S, macrolides bind 50S.
Trap two: an FIC index of two means synergy. No: synergy is one half or less. Two is indifferent.
Trap three: survival falls seven point six percent per hour in every septic patient. No: that figure comes from one retrospective septic-shock study, over the first six hours after hypotension.

scenes.title: Wall, two floors, the code, the clock
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Picture the bacterium as a building: the WALL (β-lactams, vancomycin), two ribosome FLOORS — floor 30 (aminoglycosides) and floor 50 (macrolides, clindamycin, linezolid) — and the CODE room (fluoroquinolones, rifampin, TMP-SMX, metronidazole). Quarter plus quarter makes a half: synergy. The shock clock starts at hypotension.” Tokens: wall · 30 / 50 floors · code room · ¼ + ¼ = ½. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the bacterium is a building. The wall is for beta-lactams and vancomycin. Two ribosome floors: thirty for aminoglycosides, fifty for macrolides, clindamycin and linezolid. The code room is for quinolones, rifampin, the folate pair and metronidazole. A quarter plus a quarter makes a half: synergy. And the shock clock starts at hypotension.

Where it breaks: ribosome drugs can be bactericidal for some species; synergy cutoffs and methods differ between laboratories and studies; and seven point six percent is an average from one observational study, not a guaranteed loss for each patient.

cues.text: Match each antibiotic class to its target, call a combination synergistic only when its FIC index is one half or less, and treat septic shock as a clock that starts at hypotension, because each hour of delay in effective antibiotics was linked to lower survival.

props.label: FICI ≤ 0.5 = synergy · shock clock starts at hypotension

explanation.what: Plain language: each antibiotic family attacks one part of the bacterium — the wall, one of two halves of the protein-making ribosome, or the machinery that copies and reads DNA. Two drugs together can work better than either alone, and the lab can measure that on a dilution grid. In septic shock, how fast an effective drug is given matters. Scientific terms: penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), D-alanyl-D-alanine, 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits, DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, RNA polymerase, dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase, prodrug reduction, bactericidal vs bacteriostatic, checkerboard, fractional inhibitory concentration (FIC) index, time-kill assay, tolerance (MBC/MIC ratio), septic shock.
explanation.why: Knowing targets explains combinations (a cell-wall drug helps an aminoglycoside get into the cell) and cross-resistance; synergy testing is sometimes asked for in hard-to-treat infections but its methods disagree; and timing data are the reason septic shock is treated as an emergency.
explanation.measure: FIC = MIC in combination ÷ MIC alone; FICI = FIC A + FIC B. Doern 2014: ≤0.5 synergy; 0.5–1 additive; 1–4 indifferent; >4 antagonism. Time-kill synergy: >2 log10 greater kill than the most active single agent, best assessed within 12 h. Tolerance (vancomycin, MRSA): commonly MBC/MIC ≥32. Kumar 2006: 79.9% survival with effective antimicrobials in the first hour after hypotension; average 7.6% lower survival for each further hour over the first 6 h. SSC 2021: immediately, ideally within 1 h of recognition, for possible septic shock or a high likelihood of sepsis; within 3 h for possible sepsis without shock if concern for infection persists.
explanation.differs: 30S (aminoglycosides, broadly bactericidal) vs 50S (macrolides, typically bacteriostatic); synergy (≤0.5) vs additive vs indifferent vs antagonism (>4); MIC (inhibition) vs MBC (killing) and tolerance (high MBC/MIC); septic shock (strong time association) vs sepsis without shock (weaker).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: match a drug to its target, compute an FIC index from MICs, recognise MBC/MIC ≥32 as tolerance, or recall the 7.6% per hour figure and its setting.

questions.stem: Which antibiotic class binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and is the broadly bactericidal group among ribosome inhibitors?

options.rationale: Correct. Aminoglycosides bind 16S rRNA of the 30S subunit, cause misreading and are broadly bactericidal.
Incorrect. Macrolides bind the 50S subunit and are typically bacteriostatic.
Incorrect. Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, not the ribosome.
Incorrect. Vancomycin binds D-alanyl-D-alanine on cell-wall precursors.

questions.stem: In a checkerboard, drug A has an MIC of 16 µg/mL alone and 4 µg/mL in combination; drug B has an MIC of 2 µg/mL alone and 0.25 µg/mL in combination. Using the cutoffs in Doern 2014, what is the FIC index and interpretation?

options.rationale: Incorrect. The index is right, but indifference is 1–4; ≤ 0.5 is synergy.
Incorrect. This inverts the ratios (MIC alone ÷ MIC in combination). FIC is the combination MIC divided by the MIC alone.
Incorrect. This is only drug B’s FIC; the index is the sum of both drugs’ FICs.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the Kumar 2006 septic-shock timing finding?

options.text: Each hour of delay in effective antimicrobials over the first 6 h after hypotension onset was associated with an average 7.6% fall in survival
options.rationale: Correct. This retrospective study reported 79.9% survival with effective therapy in the first hour and an average 7.6% fall for each further hour over 6 h.

options.text: A randomised trial proved that each hour of delay causes a 7.6% fall in survival
options.rationale: Incorrect. The study was retrospective and observational, so it shows an association.

options.text: The same per-hour effect applies equally to sepsis without shock
options.rationale: Incorrect. The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline notes weaker, less consistent associations without shock.

options.text: Survival only begins to fall when effective therapy is delayed beyond 6 h
options.rationale: Incorrect. The fall was reported for each hour from the second hour after hypotension onset.

claims.text: Targets of β-lactams, vancomycin, aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, macrolides, clindamycin, linezolid, fluoroquinolones, rifampin, TMP-SMX and metronidazole.
Aminoglycosides broadly bactericidal; macrolides typically bacteriostatic; aminoglycoside synergy with cell-wall agents.
Checkerboard design; FIC and FICI calculation; Doern cutoffs ≤0.5, 0.5–1, 1–4, >4.
Time-kill synergy >2 log10 greater kill than the most active single agent, best judged within 12 h; no gold standard; not endorsed routinely; cutoffs vary.
Vancomycin tolerance (MRSA) commonly defined as MBC/MIC ≥32.
claims.note: One primary study stating a common definition; no guideline or standard was read.

claims.text: Kumar 2006: 79.9% survival with effective antimicrobials in the first hour after hypotension; average 7.6% fall per additional hour over the first 6 h; retrospective.
claims.note: Taken from the first author’s 2014 review; the 2006 paper was not read.

claims.text: SSC 2021 timing recommendations and observational, weaker-without-shock evidence.

Reviewer’s “≥2-log10” time-kill threshold; tolerance as “bacteriologic failure despite susceptibility”; rapid AST and stewardship as the remedy implied by the 7.6% figure; bacteriostatic labels for clindamycin and linezolid.
claims.note: Not taught as facts; sources read give >2 log10 or do not address these points.

claims.text: Scenario invented; cell and plate drawings schematic.
“Wall, two floors, the code, the clock.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 58 Hit 13 gives the 7.6%-per-hour survival loss without context. The figure is an average over the first 6 h after onset of hypotension in one retrospective septic-shock cohort (Kumar 2014 summary); SSC 2021 notes the supporting evidence is observational and the time association is weaker and less consistent in sepsis without shock (register flag rv-ch58-kumar-context).

Ch. 58 Hit 14 gives fixed synergy thresholds. Doern 2014 defines time-kill synergy as >2 log10 (not ≥2), notes there is no true gold standard and that different synergy methods do not produce comparable results, and states synergy testing cannot be recommended for routine use; other studies use different FICI cutoffs (Stein 2015: <0.8 synergy and ≥4 antagonism, with median FICI) (register flag rv-ch58-synergy-method).
The MBC/MIC ≥32 tolerance threshold was confirmed only as a “commonly defined” threshold in one primary study; no standard document was read.

morphology.note: No photographs; targets, plates and timing shown as cards.

verification.notes: 7 claims checked against Kapoor 2017, Gajdács 2017, Stein 2015, Cázares-Domínguez 2015, Kumar 2014, Evans 2021 (open full text) and Kohanski 2010, Doern 2014 (read via a page-fetch tool); 1 pending (reviewer’s ≥2-log10 wording, tolerance as clinical failure, rapid-AST rationale, clindamycin/linezolid static labels). The Kumar 2006 original was not read. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
